Jeff Cornell is a veteran music and entertainment writer, who has contributed to Variety, Billboard, Loudwire, The Hollywood Reporter, and MTV.

The Allman Brothers Band formed in Jacksonville, Florida in 1969, before establishing their home base in Macon, Georgia. The original lineup consisted of brothers Duane Allmam, on lead and slide guitar, and Gregg Allman on keyboards and vocals, alongside bassist Berry Oakley, guitarist Dickey Betts, and drummers Butch Trucks and Jai Johanny "Jaimoe" Johanson. The six-piece group blended elements of blues, jazz and country music into an expansive rock sound defined by harmonized guitars, extended improvisation, and a rich catalog of instrumental compositions.

Tragedy struck the band with the deaths of Duane Allman in 1971 and Berry Oakley in 1972, both following motorcycle accidents in Macon, Georgia, just over a year apart. The Allman Brothers persevered, creating enduring rock classics defined by melodic guitar harmonies and Gregg Allman's powerful, bluesy vocals. Despite a split in 1976 and another extended hiatus during the 1980s, the group returned in 1989 with a revitalized lineup featuring guitarist Warren Haynes and late bassist Allen Woody. Bassist Otiel Burbridge joined in 1997 and Butch Trucks in 1999, further expanding the band's musical possibilities. Throughout its history, the group crafted a rich catalog of instrumentals that showcased its melodic imagination and adventurous musicianship. These compositions often grew into extended improvisations in concert, with each member trading solos and exploring new directions. Here is every Allman Brothers Band studio instrumental song, ranked.

11
"Pegasus"
'Enlightened Rogues' (1979)

"Pegasus" is a Dickey Betts-penned instrumental and the centerpiece of 1979's Enlightened Rogues, the band's first album following its 1976 breakup. Featuring new members Dan Toler on guitar and David Goldflies on bass, the driving track balances a soaring melody and guitar harmonies. Betts' guitar work shines throughout shifting dynamics and a dramatic ending that keeps the listener engaged.

The song keeps the listener guessing and charts its own course through its seven-plus minute journey, including a cool dual drum solo and a surprising conclusion. Its funky rhythmic feel captures the spirit of the late-70s, while the dual guitar work and Gregg Allman's Hammond organ connect it to the band's beginnings. "Pegasus" earned a 1980 Grammy nomination for Best Rock Instrumental Performance and is a spirited showcase for a reunited band.

10
"From the Madness of the West"
'Reach for the Sky' (1980)

Dickey Betts' "From the Madness of the West" is an overlooked Allman Brothers instrumental from the band's 1980 album Reach for the Sky. The six-plus-minute track highlights the twin guitar interplay between Betts and Dan Toler, with harmonized melodies and expressive lead passages that recall the band's earlier sound. Its arrangement packs that melodic chemistry into a more compact form than some of the group's sprawling instrumental epics.

Reach for the Sky was ABB's first album for Arista Records and leaned toward shorter songs and a more commercial sound. "From the Madness of the West" preserves the group's adventurous instrumental spirit, offering a rewarding showcase for Betts and Toler amid an uneven chapter in the band's history.

9
"True Gravity"
'Seven Turns' (1990)

"True Gravity" is a nearly eight-minute instrumental co-written by Dickey Betts and Warren Haynes for 1990s Seven Turns. It marks the band's first studio release following its 1989 reunion, adding Haynes, bassist Allen Woody and keyboardist Johnny Neel. The track emphasizes the group's jazz influence and renewed instrumental chemistry alongside a strong melodic voice. It was captured at the beginning of the guitar partnership between Betts and Haynes that breathed new life into the Allman Brothers Band.

The track dives deep into its jazz influence with an Ornette Coleman-inspired arrangement before rising into an uplifting and spiritually energetic tune with what nearly sounds like a tease of the band's instrumental hit "Jessica" towards the end. "True Gravity" received a 1991 Grammy nomination for Best Rock Instrumental Performance. It represents a revived band carrying on an instrumental tradition through the Betts and Haynes partnership.

8
"High Falls"
'Win, Lose or Draw' (1975)

"High Falls" is Dickie Betts' sprawling fourteen-minute composition from 1975's Win, Lose or Draw. It showcases the band's mid-1970s lineup with pianist Chuck Leavell and bassist Lamar Williams, as Leavell's piano work provides a melodic counterpart to Betts' guitar. Flowing rhythms anchored by Jamioe and Butch Trucks' drumming give Betts and Leavell ample room to explore.

"High Falls" was named for a state park in Georgia, where Betts said he composed the piece beside a waterfall. Its sweeping scope and shifting dynamics create a musical journey, with a relaxed, free-flowing atmosphere that highlights the band's jazz influence and ensemble interplay. The expansive dialogue between Betts' guitar and Leavell's piano remains an enduring highlight of the group's mid-70s work.

7
"Little Martha"
'Eat a Peach' (1972)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F6980d5dc4c66d-JC%20Logo.png?fit=crop&w=90&h=90

"Little Martha" is the delicate acoustic instrumental that closes The Allman Brothers Band's 1972 double LP Eat a Peach. At just over two minutes in length, it's the only composition credited solely to Duane Allman and was recorded in October 1971, just weeks before his tragic death. It features Allman and Dickey Betts on acoustic guitars in an open E tuning.

Its gently bouncing rhythm and warm acoustic arpeggios combine to create a beautiful song with intricate harmonies. The beauty of "Little Martha" lies in its intimacy, tenderness and guitar interplay, which reveals Duane's melodic imagination and his musical connection with Betts.

6
"Instrumental Illness"
'Hittin' The Note' (2003)

"Instrumental Illness" is the 12-minute track from the Allman Brothers Band's final studio album, Hittin' The Note. Written by guitarist Warren Haynes and bassist Otiel Burbridge, it showcases an adventurous, jazz-oriented side of the band's latter lineup. The song blends blues rock riffs, a funky rhythmic foundation and jazzy improvisation.

The upbeat track features an intense walking bass line, incredible slide guitar playing from Butch Trucks and blistering solos from Haynes. It shifts through extended solos in the exploratory tradition of other ABB instrumentals, like "In Memory of Elizabeth Reed." "Instrumental Illness" earned two Grammy nominations, one for the studio version in 2004 and another for the live rendition from One Way Out in 2005. It stands as a strong example of the Allman Brothers continuing to create ambitious new music more than three decades into their career.

5
"Kind of Bird"
'Shades of Two Worlds' (1991)

"Kind of Bird" is a jazz-influenced instrumental written by Dickey Betts and Warren Haynes for the band's 1991 LP Shades of Two Worlds. The track showcases the interplay between the two guitarists and the band's ambitious appetite for improvisation. The title honors jazz saxophonist Charlie "Bird" Parker, who influenced Betts' jazzy opening riff.

The piece shifts from a swinging jazz-inspired riff into a Latin-flavored section driven by percussionist Marc Quinones. The changing rhythmic feel gives the guitarists room to explore while keeping the arrangement moving forward with intricate harmonies and extended solos. The middle section of the song seems to fall a part and hopelessly float along, before finding footing and rising out of the ashes like a phoenix back into the main theme, giving listeners a taste of what it was like to see ABB live in the early 90s. "Kind of Bird" earned a Grammy nomination in 1992 for Best Rock Instrumental Performance, losing to Eric Johnson's "Cliffs of Dover." It's a compelling example of how The Allman Brothers Band could combine blues, jazz and Latin sounds into its melodic driving rock sensibility.

4
"Les Brers in A Minor"
'Eat a Peach' (1972)

"Les Brers in A Minor" is Dickey Betts' nine-minute instrumental, which was recorded after Duane Allman's death. It features the five surviving members of the group, with Betts on guitar, Gregg Allman on organ, Berry Oakley on bass and Butch Trucks and Jaimoe on drums. The track was recorded at Criteria Studios in Miami, Florida and is featured on the 1972 double LP Eat a Peach.

The piece opens with over three minutes of spacious and ambient jamming before settling into a driving bass groove and a focused guitar and organ melody. Betts' fluid leads combined with Gregg Allman's organ and the interlocking drumming erupts into an exploration of blues, rock and jazz. The main theme of the song was culled from a passage Betts had played during a live performance of the band's classic "Whipping Post." "Les Brers in A Minor" captures the band finding strength in collective playing during a devastating period. The expansive and forceful instrumental demonstrates how the band would carry on without brother Duane.

3
"Don't Want You No More"
'The Allman Brothers Band (1969)

One of the most powerful statements a debut album can make, "Don't Want You No More" leaps out of the speakers with its iconic guitar harmonies and a punchy riff. It's a cover of a Spencer Davis Group song, written by Spencer Davis and Eddie Hardin and originally released in 1967 with vocals. The tightly focused two-and-a-half minute song serves as a great introduction to the Georgia-based rockers.

The Allman Brothers Band makes the song its own with brief and elegant solos from organist Gregg Allman and guitarists Duane Allman and Dickey Betts. The twin guitar harmonies attack the main theme, carrying the song's vocal melody. It showcases the band's heavy blues sound and its immediate musical chemistry. As the track stumbles to its finale, it transitions into the slow blues song "It's Not My Cross to Bear," making the two tracks seem like a single dramatic introduction to the band.

2
"Jessica"
'Brothers and Sister (1973)

"Jessica" is the joyous, seven-plus-minute instrumental from 1973's Brothers and Sisters. One of the band's defining recordings, it peaked at number 65 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart and became a staple of FM rock radio. It combines Dickey Betts' instantly memorable guitar melody with Chuck Leavell's sparkling piano and Gregg Allman's Hammond organ.

Betts named the song after his young daughter, whose playful movements helped him shape the melody. He also conceived it as a tribute to Django Reinhardt, challenging himself to develop a melody playable with only two fretting fingers, reflecting the jazz guitarist's technique after a severe hand injury. Chuck Leavell's extended piano solo is central to the song's uplifting nature, while Betts' guitar passages blend melodic clarity with improvisation. "Jessica" exemplifies Betts' ability to make an extended instrumental feel as immediate and memorable as a great pop song. A live version released on 1995's An Evening with the Allman Brothers Band: 2nd Set, won Best Rock Instrumental Performance at the 1996 Grammys.
